sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Stabilization of Severe Anaphylaxis
sections.description: This section introduces the case through a structured clinical narrative, detailing the patient's history, the precipitating allergen (clarithromycin), and the immediate life-threatening symptoms. It focuses on the application of standard emergency protocols, highlighting the discrepancy between recommended adult epinephrine dosing (0.5 mg) and the actual administration of auto-injectors (0.3 mg), while emphasizing the critical role of rapid assessment and initial resuscitation.
subtopics: Patient demographics and relevant comorbidities (Diabetes HTN, Psoriasis)
Identification of the trigger: Switch from Clindamycin to Clarithromycin
Symptom evolution: Cutaneous, respiratory, cardiovascular, and neurological involvement
Initial hemodynamic instability: Hypotension and hypoxemia metrics
Standard Emergency Department management: IM Epinephrine, Antihistamines, Fluids, Oxygen
Critical analysis of epinephrine dosing: 0.3 mg vs. 0.5 mg considerations

sections.section_title: Defining Biphasic and Multiphasic Anaphylaxis: Pathophysiology and Diagnostic Challenges
sections.description: Moving beyond simple symptom recognition, this section establishes the theoretical framework for understanding why symptoms recur. It differentiates between biphasic/multiphasic courses, refractory anaphylaxis, and sustained anaphylaxis caused by ongoing allergen absorption. The text explores the proposed mechanisms of relapse (e.g., continued mediator release from mast cells) and reviews current epidemiological data regarding incidence rates and risk factors.
subtopics: Definitions: Biphasic vs. Multiphasic vs. Refractory Anaphylaxis
Pathophysiological mechanisms of symptom recurrence without re-exposure
Epidemiology: Incidence rates (4-6%) versus reported ranges (0.4-23%)
Differentiation from other causes of post-anaphylactic deterioration
Current gaps in defining 'safe' observation windows for discharge

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning in Complex Relapsing Courses and Underlying Etiologies
sections.description: This section details the clinical reasoning process triggered by multiple relapses despite adequate initial treatment. It covers the decision-making involved in escalating care to the ICU versus maintaining a conservative approach. Crucially, it addresses the investigation into secondary causes for severe/repeated reactions, specifically focusing on Systemic Mastocytosis (SM), including the interpretation of elevated tryptase levels, limitations in biopsy sampling against WHO criteria, and associated physical findings like hepatomegaly.
subtopics: Indications for ICU transfer after first relapse in an acute ward setting
Diagnostic dilemma: Evaluating for Systemic Mastocytosis in anaphylaxis survivors
"Tryptase kinetics": Timing of samples relative to symptom peaks vs. guidelines (24h+ baseline)
"WHO Criteria" application challenges: Major criteria missing vs. Minor criteria presence
"Ancillary findings": Hepatomegaly on ultrasound and neuropsychiatric correlations
